bibl.title: Disentangling perceptual awareness from nonconscious processing in rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta)
bibl.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: Whether rhesus monkeys show the opposite performance signatures that in humans distinguish conscious from nonconscious processing.
span.quote: To examine nonconscious influence in monkeys, we adopted a spatial-cueing paradigm ( 37 – 40 ).

span.label: Since a nonverbal animal cannot report what it is aware of, is there any behavioural test that can tell conscious from nonconscious processing in one?
span.quote: Since nonverbal species cannot report their internal states, philosophers and scientists have long debated whether the question of animal consciousness is empirically testable, and it still remains a topic of speculation ( 1 , 2 ).

span.label: Turns a human double dissociation into a nonverbal test of awareness, and finds the same opposite signatures in monkeys - which is evidence for two distinct processing modes without requiring a report.
span.quote: Because this approach predicts that completely opposite signatures of performance would emerge only if there were both conscious and nonconscious processing modes, this framework can be used to reliably disentangle the two levels of processing in a nonhuman animal.

span.label: existence
span.quote: These results provide robust evidence for two distinct modes of processing in nonhuman primates.

span.label: double dissociation of visual awareness in nonhuman primates
span.quote: We harnessed a well-established cross-over double dissociation between nonconscious and conscious processing, in which people perform in completely opposite ways when they are aware of stimuli versus when they are not.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: In a series of seven experiments, we first established these signatures in humans using both known and newly developed nonverbal double-dissociation tasks and then identified similar signatures in rhesus monkeys ( Macaca mulatta).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Subliminal cues capture gaze toward the cued (wrong) side and, without awareness, the subject cannot disengage before target onset, so the eyes are still at the wrong location when the target appears and the response is slowed
span.quote: subjects still failed to move their gaze to the target location ahead of time and maintained their gaze at the cue location during the final 100 ms prior to the target appearance

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Conscious access to the cue lets the subject deploy a deliberate strategy that redirects gaze to the opposite location before the target appears, converting the same cue from interference into facilitation
span.quote: suggesting again that a conscious strategy was necessary in order for participants to redirect their gaze to the relevant location.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because the two conditions push performance in opposite directions, the cross-over pattern itself is what separates aware from unaware processing in a nonverbal subject
span.quote: Since these opposite patterns of performance are predicted to emerge only if animals are aware in one condition (presenting functional facilitation) but unaware in the other (presenting persistent interference), they allow us to successfully disentangle the two types of processing in nonhuman species.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: a subliminal cue cannot be disengaged from, so it drags attention the wrong way; a supraliminal one can be reasoned about, so it helps - the two pull in opposite directions
span.quote: Researchers have argued that this phenomenon stems from the difficulty of disregarding a stimulus that is nonconsciously processed ( 33 , 34 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the design's force comes from predicting the REVERSE of what salience alone would predict, so a confound cannot produce the result
span.quote: our predictions for implicating visual awareness and nonconscious processing are predicted in the reverse direction of what would typically be expected when inhibiting salient versus nonsalient incongruent stimuli

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: only two processing modes can produce two opposite signatures, so the crossing itself is the inference - not either half of it
span.quote: Because this approach predicts that completely opposite signatures of performance would emerge only if there were both conscious and nonconscious processing modes, this framework can be used to reliably disentangle the two levels of processing in a nonhuman animal.

span.label: Awareness in monkeys could not be probed verbally, so the inference rests on the behavioural pattern alone.
span.quote: While of course we could not linguistically probe awareness in monkeys, monkeys displayed similar incongruent responses that required awareness in humans and critically also showed similar opposite performance with subliminal cues.

span.label: No subjective reports were collected from the monkeys; the subliminal thresholds were imported from the human procedure.
span.quote: While we have not specifically collected the monkeys’ subjective reports, we employed the exact same subliminal thresholds as in humans.

span.label: The nonconscious effect may arise from low-level attentional orienting or residual visual traces rather than from a richer nonconscious process.
span.quote: Whereas the nonconscious effect demonstrated here may possibly be generated by low-level nonconscious orienting of attention or from the subliminal cues’ leftover visual traces, it should be noted that it critically influenced free behavioral choices without participants awareness in both humans and monkeys.

span.label: The inference rests on a behavioural signature, not on any access to experience - the explanatory gap the paper cites is not closed by it.
span.quote: For many, the “explanatory gap” in evidence that is needed to unambiguously infer animal consciousness is considered “as wide as ever” ( 32 ).

span.label: Awareness of the subliminal cue is established by self-report and a forced-choice test, both of which are null results rather than proof of absence.
span.quote: Participants’ performance did not differ from chance at the individual binomial level or at the group level

span.label: The whole approach assumes the human dissociation transfers to another species; before this paper there was no evidence it does.
span.quote: To date, we have no evidence for such a double dissociation with opposite predictions of awareness in other species.

span.label: They take the cross-over double-dissociation marker of nonconscious processing, developed and validated only in verbal human subjects, and transplant it into nonhuman-primate comparative research as a nonverbal test for awareness
span.quote: Critically, by importing one of the strictest indicators of genuine nonconscious processing in human studies

span.label: the cross-over double dissociation of visual awareness, rebuilt as a nonverbal saccade task so that it can be run on a species that cannot be asked what it saw
span.quote: Much work in human cognitive science has shown that under certain circumstances, people display opposite behavioral signatures when they are consciously aware of stimuli (i.e., when they are exposed to clearly visible stimuli—supraliminal stimuli) versus when they are not aware (i.e., when they are exposed to stimuli that are flashed for a few milliseconds on the screen—subliminal stimuli).

span.label: two NONPREDICTIVE cues, presented in both the supraliminal and the subliminal conditions
span.quote: As a control, we also presented two nonpredictive cues, both in the supraliminal and subliminal conditions.

span.label: double dissociation
span.quote: We harnessed a well-established cross-over double dissociation between nonconscious and conscious processing, in which people perform in completely opposite ways when they are aware of stimuli versus when they are not.

span.label: single dissociations
span.quote: All these important single dissociations of awareness exploration convincingly show that animals display properties similar to those seen in conscious or nonconscious processes.

span.label: subliminal
span.quote: Critically, the target is preceded by a cue presented either supraliminally (for 250 ms) or subliminally (17/33 ms) in the opposite location, long before the target appearance

span.label: supraliminal
span.quote: Critically, the target is preceded by a cue presented either supraliminally (for 250 ms) or subliminally (17/33 ms) in the opposite location, long before the target appearance

span.label: nonconscious processing
span.quote: Researchers have argued that this phenomenon stems from the difficulty of disregarding a stimulus that is nonconsciously processed ( 33 , 34 ).

span.label: visual awareness
span.quote: Taken together, these results strongly support the existence of both nonconscious processing as well as functional human-like visual awareness in nonhuman animals.

span.label: spatial-cueing paradigm
span.quote: To examine nonconscious influence in monkeys, we adopted a spatial-cueing paradigm ( 37 – 40 ).

span.label: explanatory gap
span.quote: For many, the “explanatory gap” in evidence that is needed to unambiguously infer animal consciousness is considered “as wide as ever” ( 32 ).

span.label: theory of mind
span.quote: some advocate that consciousness may require complex processes like language, which is unique to adult humans ( 3 ) or a human-like theory of mind ( 4 )

span.label: awareness - the reportable kind, defined operationally by what a subject says it saw and by a forced-choice test at chance
span.quote: Participants’ performance did not differ from chance at the individual binomial level or at the group level

span.label: awareness - the behavioural kind, defined by a crossing of two opposite performance signatures and requiring no report at all
span.quote: Because this approach predicts that completely opposite signatures of performance would emerge only if there were both conscious and nonconscious processing modes, this framework can be used to reliably disentangle the two levels of processing in a nonhuman animal.

span.label: consciousness - the demanding sense requiring language or theory of mind, which would confine it to humans and a few great apes
span.quote: some advocate that consciousness may require complex processes like language, which is unique to adult humans ( 3 ) or a human-like theory of mind ( 4 )

span.label: consciousness - the neuroanatomical sense, on which birds and octopuses may qualify
span.quote: In contrast, based on neuroanatomical similarities, some argue that a number of species (including some birds and octopuses) are likely to be capable of generating conscious experience ( 7 ).

span.label: extends → the single-dissociation literature on animal awareness (blindsight analogues, implicit/explicit memory, binocular rivalry)
span.quote: All these important single dissociations of awareness exploration convincingly show that animals display properties similar to those seen in conscious or nonconscious processes.

span.label: contradicts → the position that consciousness requires language or a human-like theory of mind
span.quote: some advocate that consciousness may require complex processes like language, which is unique to adult humans ( 3 ) or a human-like theory of mind ( 4 )

span.label: builds-on → the spatial-cueing paradigm ( 37 - 40 )
span.quote: To examine nonconscious influence in monkeys, we adopted a spatial-cueing paradigm ( 37 – 40 ).

span.label: visual awareness —operationalised-as→ double dissociation
span.quote: Because this approach predicts that completely opposite signatures of performance would emerge only if there were both conscious and nonconscious processing modes, this framework can be used to reliably disentangle the two levels of processing in a nonhuman animal.

span.label: subliminal —contrasted-with→ supraliminal
span.quote: Much work in human cognitive science has shown that under certain circumstances, people display opposite behavioral signatures when they are consciously aware of stimuli (i.e., when they are exposed to clearly visible stimuli—supraliminal stimuli) versus when they are not aware (i.e., when they are exposed to stimuli that are flashed for a few milliseconds on the screen—subliminal stimuli).

span.label: visual awareness —distinct-from→ nonconscious processing
span.quote: We harnessed a well-established cross-over double dissociation between nonconscious and conscious processing, in which people perform in completely opposite ways when they are aware of stimuli versus when they are not.

span.label: nonconscious processing —operationalised-as→ subliminal
span.quote: Critically, the target is preceded by a cue presented either supraliminally (for 250 ms) or subliminally (17/33 ms) in the opposite location, long before the target appearance

span.label: linear mixed model
span.quote: All statistics were performed on log response time for correct responses using linear mixed models

span.label: F-test
span.quote: Participants were faster with supraliminal cues than with subliminal cues [ F (1,3585) = 315.66, P < 0.0001].

span.label: correlation
span.quote: This facilitation improved with time as indicated by the interaction of cue type with experimental trials [ F (2,3585) = 167.06, P < 0.0001; r = −0.86, P < 0.001].

span.label: binomial test
span.quote: we compared individuals’ binomial test’s P values of each participant against chance and examined if more participants than expected had obtained binomial P values in the most extreme lowest quartile as a group.

span.label: chi-squared test
span.quote: regardless of response modality [χ (1) = 5.33, P = 0.021], suggesting that more participants than expected were performing markedly below chance

span.label: chi-squared test
span.quote: scoring significantly well above chance [χ (3) = 16.67, P < 0.001, Fig. 4 A ]

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Error bars denote SEM of monkey trials.

span.label: mean and standard deviation
span.quote: Participants successfully performed the task in the supraliminal condition, reliably choosing the target opposite to the cue (mean= 94.6% correct, SD = 3.7% in the eye-tracking modality and mean= 94.6%, SD = 3.5% in the key-press modality).

span.label: learning-slope correlation
span.quote: Participants also showed no signs of learning in the subliminal condition [flat learning slope, mean r(383) = 0.005, P = 0.92].

span.label: anova
span.quote: participants were considerably faster to identify the target location following supraliminal incongruent cues than subliminal incongruent cues of which they reported not being aware [ F (1,3585) = 315.66, P < 0.0001, Fig. 1 B ]

span.label: statistical-significance
span.quote: all of the participants performing in the subliminal condition, regardless of block order, reported that they did not see any cues § yet showed a significant slowdown in detecting the target location compared to the baseline with two nonpredictive subliminal cues [ F (1,2989) = 13.36, P < 0.0001, Fig. 1 C , Left ]

span.label: binomial-test
span.quote: Participants’ performance did not differ from chance at the individual binomial level or at the group level

span.label: Subliminal incongruent cues slowed human target detection relative to baseline even though participants reported and tested as unaware of them, establishing nonconscious processing.
span.quote: The observation that subliminal cues significantly hindered the detection of the targets relative to baseline, even though participants were unaware of the cues or their locations, demonstrates that these cues were processed nonconsciously.

span.label: Rhesus monkeys showed the identical subliminal slowdown relative to the nonpredictive-cue baseline in the spatial-cueing task.
span.quote: Critically, however, when the monkeys were tested in the subliminal condition, they were significantly slower to detect the target location compared to the control baseline condition with two nonpredictive subliminal cues

span.label: In the forced-guessing task monkeys performed below chance under subliminal cueing and never learned the rule, mirroring the human pattern.
span.quote: Just as we observed in human participants, monkeys failed to ignore the subliminal cues and showed no signs of learning

span.label: Human supraliminal facilitation depended on consciously grasping the cue's predictive rule; participants who did not report that insight showed no speed-up over baseline.
span.quote: In contrast, participants in the same supraliminal condition, who reported that they were not aware of the supraliminal cue’s predictive value, were not facilitated (mean = 324 ms) relative to baseline (mean = 312 ms)

span.label: Merely telling participants that flashing cues exist flipped their performance, showing that awareness of the cue and not its low salience is what drives the effect.
span.quote: This suggests that cue awareness rather than cue saliency (which remained constantly difficult to see, here at 33 ms) is the critical factor in performance on our studies.

span.label: Within the same participants and the same 17 ms cue, trials rated as unseen produced below-chance performance while trials rated as seen produced above-chance performance.
span.quote: Remarkably, participants’ performance was still significantly below chance when they reported no awareness of where the cue was presented (0 rating)

span.label: The headline result is that a nonhuman primate reproduces the human double-dissociation signature, which the authors read as evidence for two distinct processing modes in monkeys.
span.quote: We found that one nonhuman species—the rhesus monkey—exhibits a double-dissociation performance remarkably similar to that observed in humans.

span.label: Humans are much faster with a visible incongruent cue than with an invisible one - the conscious condition helps.
span.quote: participants were considerably faster to identify the target location following supraliminal incongruent cues than subliminal incongruent cues of which they reported not being aware [ F (1,3585) = 315.66, P < 0.0001, Fig. 1 B ]

span.label: The same cue presented invisibly does the opposite: participants who saw nothing were nevertheless slowed relative to baseline.
span.quote: all of the participants performing in the subliminal condition, regardless of block order, reported that they did not see any cues § yet showed a significant slowdown in detecting the target location compared to the baseline with two nonpredictive subliminal cues [ F (1,2989) = 13.36, P < 0.0001, Fig. 1 C , Left ]

span.label: Rhesus monkeys show the same two opposite signatures, which is the paper's basis for two processing modes in a nonhuman species.
span.quote: In a series of seven experiments, we first established these signatures in humans using both known and newly developed nonverbal double-dissociation tasks and then identified similar signatures in rhesus monkeys ( Macaca mulatta).

span.label: Earlier work established only single dissociations, which show animals have properties resembling conscious or nonconscious processing without separating the two.
span.quote: All these important single dissociations of awareness exploration convincingly show that animals display properties similar to those seen in conscious or nonconscious processes.

span.label: supraliminal versus subliminal stimuli
span.quote: Much work in human cognitive science has shown that under certain circumstances, people display opposite behavioral signatures when they are consciously aware of stimuli (i.e., when they are exposed to clearly visible stimuli—supraliminal stimuli) versus when they are not aware (i.e., when they are exposed to stimuli that are flashed for a few milliseconds on the screen—subliminal stimuli).

span.label: cross-over double dissociation of awareness
span.quote: We harnessed a well-established cross-over double dissociation between nonconscious and conscious processing, in which people perform in completely opposite ways when they are aware of stimuli versus when they are not.

span.label: spatial-cueing paradigm
span.quote: In this task, a target appears in one of two locations and participants are requested to identify the target location as quickly as possible.

span.label: forced-guessing paradigm
span.quote: We thus modified the task to be a forced-guessing paradigm in which monkeys and humans had to choose which of two simultaneous targets contained a reward.

span.label: the double-dissociation logic as a test for two processing modes
span.term: the double-dissociation logic as a test for two processing modes
span.quote: Because this approach predicts that completely opposite signatures of performance would emerge only if there were both conscious and nonconscious processing modes, this framework can be used to reliably disentangle the two levels of processing in a nonhuman animal.

span.label: supraliminal and subliminal stimuli
span.quote: Much work in human cognitive science has shown that under certain circumstances, people display opposite behavioral signatures when they are consciously aware of stimuli (i.e., when they are exposed to clearly visible stimuli—supraliminal stimuli) versus when they are not aware (i.e., when they are exposed to stimuli that are flashed for a few milliseconds on the screen—subliminal stimuli).

span.label: cross-over double dissociation
span.quote: We harnessed a well-established cross-over double dissociation between nonconscious and conscious processing, in which people perform in completely opposite ways when they are aware of stimuli versus when they are not.

span.label: the word-stem completion task
span.quote: human participants are asked to complete a word stem (e.g., “SPI __ ”) without using a reference word that had been flashed on the screen just before it (e.g., “SPICE”)

span.label: cue visibility condition (supraliminal 250 ms vs subliminal 17/33 ms)
span.term: cue visibility condition (supraliminal 250 ms vs subliminal 17/33 ms)
span.quote: Critically, the target is preceded by a cue presented either supraliminally (for 250 ms) or subliminally (17/33 ms) in the opposite location, long before the target appearance

span.label: species tested (humans vs rhesus monkeys)
span.quote: In a series of seven experiments, we first established these signatures in humans using both known and newly developed nonverbal double-dissociation tasks and then identified similar signatures in rhesus monkeys

span.label: response time to locate the target
span.term: response time to locate the target
span.quote: Participants were faster with supraliminal cues than with subliminal cues [ F (1,3585) = 315.66, P < 0.0001].

span.label: accuracy relative to chance in the forced-guessing task
span.term: accuracy relative to chance in the forced-guessing task
span.quote: This pattern of below-chance performance would indicate that the subliminal stimuli were indeed processed nonconsciously and that they affected performance in a nonrandom fashion.

span.label: gaze frequency at the cued versus uncued location
span.term: gaze frequency at the cued versus uncued location
span.quote: We measured the monkeys’ gaze frequencies (mean duration of gaze across trials) in the cue location and the opposite no-cue location.

span.label: two nonpredictive cues baseline condition
span.quote: As a control, we also presented two nonpredictive cues, both in the supraliminal and subliminal conditions.

span.label: self-reported awareness of the cue's predictive value
span.term: self-reported awareness of the cue's predictive value
span.quote: In contrast, participants in the same supraliminal condition, who reported that they were not aware of the supraliminal cue’s predictive value, were not facilitated (mean = 324 ms) relative to baseline (mean = 312 ms)

span.label: cue visibility - supraliminal (250 ms) or subliminal (17/33 ms)
span.term: cue visibility - supraliminal (250 ms) or subliminal (17/33 ms)
span.quote: Critically, the target is preceded by a cue presented either supraliminally (for 250 ms) or subliminally (17/33 ms) in the opposite location, long before the target appearance

span.label: response time to locate the target, relative to a nonpredictive-cue baseline
span.term: response time to locate the target, relative to a nonpredictive-cue baseline
span.quote: participants were considerably faster to identify the target location following supraliminal incongruent cues than subliminal incongruent cues of which they reported not being aware [ F (1,3585) = 315.66, P < 0.0001, Fig. 1 B ]

span.label: mean = 43.5% correct, P = 0.00018 — Monkeys' below-chance accuracy in the subliminal forced-guessing condition and its combined binomial probability
span.quote: but critically performed significantly below-chance level in the subliminal condition (mean = 43.5% correct, with a combined binomial probability of P = 0.00018

span.label: 42% versus 25% — Share of human participants falling in the lowest binomial p-value quartile versus the share expected by chance
span.quote: there were significantly more participants in the lowest P value quartile (42%) than expected by chance (25%) regardless of response modality

span.label: 94.6% correct, SD = 3.7% — Human accuracy in the supraliminal forced-guessing condition (eye-tracking modality)
span.quote: Participants successfully performed the task in the supraliminal condition, reliably choosing the target opposite to the cue (mean= 94.6% correct, SD = 3.7% in the eye-tracking modality and mean= 94.6%, SD = 3.5% in the key-press modality).

span.label: 4 monkeys, 145 humans — Total subjects across the seven experiments
span.quote: Data for our experiments were collected from 4 adult rhesus monkeys ( Macaca mulatta ) and 145 human subjects.

span.label: 75% — Participants who became aware of the cues and used them when only 20% of trials carried a supraliminal cue
span.quote: We found that even in this design the majority of participants (75%) became aware of the cues and used them efficiently to choose the opposite target

span.label: 250 ms versus 17/33 ms — Cue exposure durations defining the supraliminal and subliminal conditions
span.quote: Critically, the target is preceded by a cue presented either supraliminally (for 250 ms) or subliminally (17/33 ms) in the opposite location, long before the target appearance

span.label: 1.2% — Human error rate, which did not differ between supraliminal and subliminal conditions
span.quote: Error rates were low (1.2%) and did not differ significantly between the supraliminal and subliminal conditions.

span.label: 50% — Chance level in the forced-guessing task, above which performance requires using the incongruent cue
span.quote: In order to find the reward with more than 50% accuracy (chance level), participants have to use the incongruent cue.

span.label: 250 ms vs 17/33 ms — supraliminal versus subliminal cue durations - the manipulation the whole design turns on
span.quote: Critically, the target is preceded by a cue presented either supraliminally (for 250 ms) or subliminally (17/33 ms) in the opposite location, long before the target appearance

span.label: seven experiments — size of the series, humans then monkeys
span.quote: In a series of seven experiments, we first established these signatures in humans using both known and newly developed nonverbal double-dissociation tasks and then identified similar signatures in rhesus monkeys ( Macaca mulatta).

span.label: 200 ms fixation — gaze hold required to register a response, the nonverbal substitute for a button press
span.quote: Participants needed to saccade and hold their fixation for 200 ms on the chosen target in order to select it.
